11666e6npoo: decentrek explained EIP-8288 in plain language. Ethereum scales along three dimensions, execution (gas), blobs (DA) and state, and 8288 scales a fourth dimension, proof verification. In a PQ environment, verifying signatures directly is too expensive and they must be aggregated with a STARK, but a PQ STARK is about 512kb and costs millions of gas to verify. Single aggregation by the block builder creates a builder bottleneck and mempool bandwidth problems, so the proposal is for each mempool node to aggregate locally and gossip aggregated proofs instead of raw signatures. decentrek argued that as more nodes join, more signatures can be aggregated, so decentralization makes scaling easier rather than harder. However, whether mempool nodes have enough compute to aggregate is still unresolved, and there are no benchmarks.

1pi9b0m45to: GottfriedHerold proposed an encrypted mempool design based on threshold IBE that removes the batch decryption requirement, posting it on ethresear.ch. Users first submit an onchain ticket, a hiding commitment to the actual transaction, which pins execution to a future block. The hash of the block that includes the ticket is used as the IBE identity, which mitigates replay during reorgs. The pipeline has a fixed two-block delay: ticket inclusion, PTC votes and bitfield commitment, key share release, then top-of-block execution of the decryption transaction. Because of this, a builder cannot see the decrypted content before deciding on inclusion. The design also includes a circuit breaker that turns the mempool off and refunds reserved gas if decryption fails for a prolonged period. The author names the hardest open problem as the requirements themselves, in particular finding a threshold IBE scheme that is also quantum-resistant.

ChainSecurity found that the gas cost changes in EIP-8037 and 8038 allow transactions that were previously invalid to attack existing contracts, and potential vulnerability was confirmed in 13 major DeFi projects. Read together with lex_node opening a debate the same day that 'L2s benefit the crypto industry but are merely a less bad competitor to Ethereum itself', the premise that 'L2s follow L1 standards' has broken, and a structure in which each builds the standard that fits its own market has been formalized.
